1:
The third and final round of the debate opens with the flattest of formulas, "Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said," and the witnesses agree that behind its calm lies the ugliest turn the friends have yet taken. The reformed John Gill observes that Eliphaz, as the first and perhaps the oldest of the three, leads every fresh course of the dispute; but here, instead of replying to Job's arguments and instances, at which he was very angry, he betakes himself to calumny and reproach, drawing invidious consequences where he ought to have brought solid reasons for conviction. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the same descent: Eliphaz proceeds in a far more exaggerated and offensive tone than he has yet adopted, accusing Job of definite and specific crimes, and he opens by asserting that the judgment of God must be wholly disinterested, so that if God rewards or punishes there can be nothing personal in it.

The latin-fathers Gregory the Great reads the opening move as the reflex of a man losing an argument. Those who get the worst in making out a case, he says, often repeat even what is well known, lest by holding their tongue they should seem defeated; and so Eliphaz, pressed closely by the sayings of blessed Job, utters things of which no one is ignorant. By comparison with God, Gregory adds, our knowledge is but ignorance, for it is by participation and not by comparison with God that we are imbued with wisdom; and in all that we do well we are doing good to ourselves and not to God, as the Psalmist owns, "Thou needest not my goods" (Ps. 16:2).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry is careful to sort the true doctrine from its false application. Eliphaz insinuates that, because Job complained so much of his afflictions, he thought God unjust in afflicting him; but this, Henry says, was a strained innuendo, for Job was far from thinking so. What Eliphaz urges is therefore unjustly applied to Job, yet in itself very true and good: that when God does us good it is not because he is indebted to us, and that no man by any meritorious action can make God his debtor (Rom. 11:35). Man's piety, Henry grants with Eliphaz, is no profit to God, no gain; the gains of religion are infinitely greater than its losses, and God is a sovereign who gives no account of his conduct, yet approves the likeness of his own holiness and accepts the thankful services of the humble believer while rejecting the proud claim of the self-confident. The witnesses do not divide: they agree that the words are sound in themselves and cruel in their aim, a right doctrine bent into a wrong indictment.
2:
Eliphaz presses the abstract principle into a question, "Can a man be profitable unto God?" and the witnesses gather round the strange verb that carries it. The reformed John Gill takes the drift plainly: Eliphaz imagined that Job, by insisting on his integrity and complaining of his afflictions, thought God beholden to him for his righteousness; but no man, even the best, and by the best things he can do, can be profitable to God. The good man's goodness extends not to the Lord; it comes from him and is his own already; and when he has done all that is commanded, he is bid to say, and truly, "we are unprofitable servants."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the word itself. The verb sakan, in the sense "to be profitable," is peculiar to the book of Job; its notion is best perceived from the causative form Eliphaz had just used at ch. 21:21, and it signifies originally, like a kindred root, to dwell beside, then to become accustomed to one another, to be serviceable, to be of use. They render the line, "Is a man profitable unto God? No, indeed; the intelligent man is profitable to himself" — a note worth holding, for the same verb returns at the speech's turn in v.21, where Job is bidden to "acquaint" himself with God. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the theology blunt: a man may be profitable to a man, but no man can profit his Maker; God has no interest in Job's conduct and does not punish him because he has been deprived of some good; "thy iniquities are against justice, and justice requires thy punishment." John Wesley reads the whole as a rebuke of self-importance: "Why dost thou insist so much upon thy own righteousness, as if thou didst oblige God by it?"

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, attends to the second half of the verse, where the Hebrew is cramped. "As he that is wise" he takes to be probably an independent statement, "Surely he that is wise is profitable" — that is, a wise man's wisdom returns upon himself, not upon God. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Eliphaz's premise is unimpeachable — the Almighty gains nothing from human virtue — even as they see that he means it as the first stone in a wall he is building against an innocent man, whose supposed presumption in pleading his righteousness is the very thing Eliphaz thinks he is refuting.
3:
"Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect?" — the question doubles the thought of the last verse, and the witnesses probe how far God is, and is not, pleased by human goodness. The reformed John Gill will not let the negation be pressed into a denial of all divine complacency. The Lord does take pleasure in his people, he says, not as sinners but as righteous, and as they are considered righteous in Christ, whose righteousness is imputed to them, so that they stand before him unblamable; he delights in the work of his own hands upon them, in the new man formed after his image, in the graces of his Spirit and their exercise — faith, hope, love, humility, the fear of God — and it is a pleasure to him to hear their prayers and praises and to observe their cheerful obedience. Yet all this, Gill insists, gives him no new pleasure and adds nothing to the complacency of his mind; he would have had as much delight within himself if there had never been a holy angel in heaven or a righteous man on earth.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the point to its edge. Adam Clarke states it in a line: God, infinite in his perfections, can neither gain nor lose by the wickedness or righteousness of men. John Wesley distinguishes the kind of pleasure meant — not such a pleasure as God needs for his own ease and contentment, for "God needs not us, or our services; we are undone, for ever undone, without him, but he is happy, for ever happy, without us."

The witnesses converge on a truth that cuts two ways in Eliphaz's mouth. Rightly held, it magnifies the divine condescension: that a God who can gain nothing from us should yet invite, encourage, and accept our poor services is pure grace. But Eliphaz wields it as a weapon, to prove that Job's much-vaunted integrity lays God under no obligation, and therefore that his complaint against his afflictions is groundless. Gill's careful balance keeps both halves in view — God is not indebted to the righteous, and yet is truly well pleased with them for Christ's sake — where Eliphaz, hearing only the first half, turns a comfort into a taunt against a suffering man whose only plea had been the integrity God himself had commended.
4:
From what God does not gain Eliphaz turns to what God does not fear, asking, "Will he reprove thee for fear of thee? will he enter with thee into judgment?" The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the irony. When God restrains or rebukes us, he says, it is not because he is in danger from us or jealous of us, as princes sometimes curb the growing greatness of a subject lest he become formidable. Satan indeed whispered to our first parents that God forbade them the tree of knowledge for fear they should become as gods and rival him; but it was a base insinuation. God rebukes the good because he loves them, and never rebukes the great because he fears them; he does not pick a quarrel or seek occasion against men lest they eclipse his honour. Magistrates punish offenders for fear of them, Pharaoh oppressed Israel because he feared them, and Herod slew the children of Bethlehem for fear; but God does not, as they did, pervert justice for fear of any.

The reformed John Gill takes the same sense — God does not chastise for fear that hurt should be done to him, for though sin is an act of hostility that strikes at his being and government, he is in no danger of being dethroned. But Gill records a second rendering that turns the verse the other way. The words may be read "for thy fear," that is, for thy fear of God, thy piety, or, as Broughton has it, "for thy religion"; and in that sense Eliphaz would be granting what Job had often urged, that good men who truly fear God are yet afflicted by him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the first reading, glossing it "because he standeth in awe of thee — will he justify his dealings with thee?"

The wesleyan-arminian voices round out the taunt. Adam Clarke puts it as a sarcasm: is it because God is afraid thou wilt do him some injury that he has stripped thee of thy power and wealth? John Wesley answers his own paraphrase — God does not punish thee because he is afraid lest, let alone, thou grow too great and powerful for him: "surely no; as thy righteousness cannot profit him, so thy wickedness can do him no hurt." So a slight divergence runs beneath the agreement: most read the clause of God's supposed dread of Job, and only Gill, with Broughton, lets it be heard as "for thy piety" — yet all agree the drift is that a God who neither gains nor fears has no motive to afflict but justice, which Eliphaz is about to press into a charge.
5:
Here the speech wheels from principle to accusation, and the mask comes off: "Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?" The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the moment as the one where Eliphaz finally says outright what the friends had only hinted — "Thou art the man," the tyrant, the oppressor they had been describing all along. "Is not thy wickedness great?" Henry has him reason; "certainly it is, or else thy troubles would not be so great." Strictly, Henry notes, nothing is infinite but God; yet sin, being committed against Infinite Majesty, has in it a kind of infinite malignity, so that Eliphaz means Job's sins are more than can be counted and more heinous than can be conceived. And Henry turns on the accuser: for aught we know, Eliphaz in slandering Job did him as great a wrong as the Sabeans and Chaldeans who robbed him, for a man's good name is more precious than his wealth, and innocency itself is no security against a false and foul tongue.

The reformed John Gill will not simply deny the words. It must be owned, he says, that the wickedness of every man's heart is great, desperately wicked and full of sin; some sins are greater than others, yet all are great as committed against God and as breaches of his law, and a sensible sinner owns himself the chief of sinners. But Gill is clear that the general truth is here wrongly fastened on a particular man. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the second clause with the Hebrew before him: "of thy continuance in them there is no end" — ein kets — so that the charge is not only of many and great sins but of an obstinate persistence in them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays bare the false reasoning at the root of the whole indictment. This, he says, was mere conjecture and surmise, arising from a single false assumption: that a just God can only punish the wicked, and that therefore those must be wicked whom he punishes. It is the axiom on which every specific charge that follows is built, and the very axiom the book of Job exists to overthrow. The witnesses do not divide over the fact — Eliphaz has passed from insinuation to open impeachment — but they gather to defend the accused, agreeing with Ellicott that the greatness of Job's supposed wickedness is inferred wholly backward, from his sufferings, and with Henry that to charge a man with what one cannot prove is itself a grievous sin.
6:
The indictment now descends to particulars, and the first imagined crime is a hard-hearted usury: "thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays out the charge as Eliphaz frames it — that for some inconsiderable debt Job had demanded and carried away by violence a pledge of great value, even from a brother whose honesty he could not doubt; the Septuagint, Henry notes, reads it "thou hast taken thy brethren for pledges," as if he had enslaved them for what they owed; and he had taken the very clothes of his insolvent debtors and left them naked, though the law of Moses expressly forbade keeping a poor man's garment overnight (Exod. 22:26; Deut. 24:13).

The reformed John Gill weighs the phrase "for nought." It can hardly mean for nothing at all, he says, but for a trifling sum, comparatively nothing, or for a loan so short that no pledge was needed; and to exact it, especially of a brother in nature or in religion, was unkind. He too records the alternative rendering, "thou hast taken thy brothers for a pledge," their very persons seized as security to be sold or held in bondage. And Gill raises the moral question the whole catalogue provokes: if Eliphaz spoke these things only as conjectures, inferred from Job's calamities, it was contrary to the charity that thinks no evil; and if as positive assertions of fact, they were simply false.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott says as much in a sentence: these specific charges, false as they were, show the depth to which Eliphaz had sunk. The wesleyan-arminian voices fill in the manner of the accusation. Adam Clarke reads it as a sweeping calumny — Job had been vexatious in all his dealings, exacting where nothing was due, so that through him the poor could not procure their necessary clothing. John Wesley catches the guesswork behind it, hearing Eliphaz speak "by way of strong presumption": "when I consider thy unusual calamities, I conclude thou art guilty of all, or some, of these crimes." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the charge is an invention, reasoned backward from Job's ruin, and that its very specificity — the pledge, the stripped garment, the wronged brother — is the measure of how far a well-meaning friend can fall once he begins by assuming the sufferer guilty.
7:
The catalogue turns from what Job supposedly seized to what he supposedly withheld: "thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry." The reformed John Gill feels the sting of the smallness of the thing denied. To a weary, thirsty traveller in those hot countries cold water was a great refreshment, and in the desert not to be had for the asking, since the rich kept their own wells; yet a cup of cold water is one of the least favours a man can give, and to deny it to one in distress was inhuman — and, Gill adds, very far from Job's real character. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same point from Eliphaz's side: he charges that Job was not charitable even to poor travellers, giving not so much as a cup of cold water to the weary, and withholding bread from the hungry — which is to withhold good from those to whom it is due (Prov. 3:27).

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look past the single charge to the portrait Eliphaz is painting. The "man of the arm," they explain — the strong man of the next verse — is in Eliphaz's mind Job himself, who is imagined to have gathered the land far and wide into his own hand by open violence or by cunning and unfeeling practices, so that the all-absorbing love of self regulated all his dealings. The refusal of water and bread is thus not an isolated fault but the meanness of a great man who has swallowed up his neighbours.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the custom that makes the accusation bite. It was esteemed a great virtue in the East to furnish thirsty travellers with water, especially in the deserts where a stream was scarce and wells were rare; he recalls the Indian devotees who stand on the public roads with a skin of water to give the parched wayfarer drink. Against such a background, to have refused water was to have offended the plainest law of hospitality. The witnesses do not divide; they agree both that the charge, measured against the custom of the land, is a grave one, and that it is wholly untrue of the man whom God himself had called upright — a slander that borrows the language of a real virtue only to accuse an innocent man of its opposite.
8:
A single line breaks the run of second-person accusations to describe a favoured oppressor: "but as for the mighty man, he had the earth; and the honourable man dwelt in it." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unpacks the Hebrew, ish zeroa, "the man of arm" — finger, hand, and arm all being emblems of strength — so that this is the man of power and influence, of rapine and plunder; while "the honourable man" is literally "the man whose face is accepted," the respectable man of wealth. Clarke reads the verse as a charge of favouritism: "thou wert an enemy to the poor and needy, but didst favour and flatter the rich and great."

Here the witnesses divide over whom the mighty man is. On one reading he is a third party whom Job, as judge, unjustly favoured. The reformed John Gill takes it so: when any cause came before Job as magistrate between a rich man and a poorer, he gave the cause to the mighty, so that the rich man "had the earth," the disputed land, whether it was rightly his or no. John Wesley agrees, glossing "dwelt" as "by thy sentence or permission he had a peaceable and sure possession of it, whether he had right to it or no." On the other reading the mighty man is Job himself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the arm-man Job, who looked on the land as his and must have it, planting himself firmly in it and filling it out alone, like a stout fellow who crowds all others out of room. Charles Ellicott concurs that by "the mighty and the honourable man" is probably meant Job, and sets aside the further suggestion that the words from v.5 onward are spoken by God entering into judgment, as hardly probable.

So the debate is real: does the verse accuse Job of showing partiality to the mighty, or of being the mighty man who devoured his neighbours' land? The witnesses do not resolve it, and for their common purpose they need not, for on either reading the charge is the same in kind — the abuse of power against the weak — and on either reading it is, they agree, an imagined crime, reasoned backward from Job's fallen greatness by friends determined to find a cause for his ruin. It is a bitter irony none of them fails to feel: the very rank and substance that had once been the token of Job's blessing are here made the proof of his oppression, as though greatness itself were guilt, and the honour a man once bore the surest evidence against him.
9:
"Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken" — the charge reaches the two classes the law most tenderly protects, and the witnesses feel both its cruelty and its cunning. The reformed John Gill reads it of a man who turned the helpless from his door: widows who came to a rich man for charity, or to a magistrate for justice, and went away with neither food nor redress. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry notes how Eliphaz slips the blackest stroke in by insinuation. "The arms of the fatherless have been broken," he says — and Eliphaz does not quite say "thou hast broken them," but would have it so understood; for those in power who do not relieve the oppressed are chargeable with the wrong they fail to prevent.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the thought forward to the punishment Eliphaz will draw from it. On account of this inhuman mode of action, they say, snares are round about him, as in Bildad's picture of the evil-doer's fate (ch. 18:8-10); ruin encompasses him on every side so that he sees no way out, and the approaching destruction announces itself beforehand by terrors that come suddenly upon him. The oppression of the widow and orphan is thus made the very hinge on which the whole doom of the following verses turns.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep to the plain sense of the words. Adam Clarke reads the broken arms as a total dispossession — whatever strength or property the fatherless had, Job is charged with having stripped them of it, hard-hearted and cruel, enriching himself with the spoils of the poor and defenceless. John Wesley glosses "arms" simply as "their supports and rights." The witnesses do not divide over the meaning; they agree that Eliphaz has now completed his imagined portrait of Job as the very type of the powerful oppressor — the man who robs his brother, strips the naked, starves the hungry, favours the strong, and crushes the widow and orphan — and that the whole of it is a fiction, the more wicked for being drawn in such fine and confident detail against a man his friend could not accuse of a single proven fault. And the witnesses mark how the very order of the charges mounts, from the wronged brother to the stripped debtor, the starving traveller, the favoured tyrant, and now the broken orphan, as if Eliphaz meant the sheer accumulation to carry the conviction that no single proof could ever give.
10:
With the indictment complete, Eliphaz draws his inference in a single word — "therefore": "therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee." The reformed John Gill fastens on that connective. Because of the sins just charged, he says, punishments of every kind have beset Job and hemmed him in on all sides, so that there is no way left to escape; and he reads the snares as the very calamities of the opening chapters — the Sabeans and Chaldeans that carried off the cattle, the fire from heaven that consumed the sheep, the wind that crushed the house upon his children, the boils that covered his body. The whole ruin is offered as the proof of the guilt.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the law of retribution Eliphaz assumes: as Job dealt with others, so God in his retributive providence has dealt with him; as he spoiled, so is he spoiled, taken in a net from which he cannot break free. Clarke lends the picture a vivid image from the chase — the hunting of the elephant, driven from strait to strait into a narrowing enclosure until it can go no further, and then its consternation is great and its roaring terrible; so, Eliphaz would have it, God has hunted Job down.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the accusation reach inward to the conscience. The providence of God, on Eliphaz's scheme, crosses and embarrasses such men so that snares are round about them; and their own hearts betray them, for no sin makes a louder cry within than unmercifulness, and so "sudden fear troubleth thee." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the note of terror: the coming destruction makes itself felt time after time in alarms that seize the guilty man suddenly and disconcert him, so that his mind is already tasting the ruin before it falls. The witnesses do not divide over the reading; they agree that Eliphaz has built a syllogism whose every premise is false — that Job's afflictions are the snares of a hunted oppressor, and his inward anguish the guilty fear of a bad conscience — when in truth, as the book will show, they are the trial of a good man, and the fear that troubles him the darkness of a faith under fire. The word "therefore," the witnesses observe, is the pivot of the whole speech: all that Eliphaz has invented of Job's cruelty exists only to justify this inference, that a man so afflicted must first have been a man so cruel — the conclusion sought from the beginning, now dressed out as though it had been discovered.
11:
The same doom is pictured now as blindness and flood: "or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee." The reformed John Gill offers the verse two ways. The darkness may be a judicial blindness of mind — the stupor of a man who cannot see the hand of God upon him or the snares about him — or it may be the darkness of affliction itself, a dispensation so dark that the sufferer cannot see the cause or reason of it, nor any comfort, nor any way out; and this last, Gill allows, was truly Job's case, who begged God to show him wherefore he contended with him, sitting in an inward darkness of soul deprived of the light of God's countenance as well as in the outward darkness of adversity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the connection with the previous verse hard, and suspects the text. Very probably, he says, a letter has dropped from the first word, so that what we read as "or" (au) was originally "light" (aur); the Septuagint certainly so read it, translating "thy light is changed into darkness" — that is, thy prosperity into adversity — and Houbigant would emend it to "darkness, and not light, shalt thou behold." John Wesley keeps the received text and reads the two clauses as the sum of Job's misery — troubled either with the fear of further evils or with the gross darkness of his present state, the "waters" standing, as often, for a flood of sore afflictions.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the little clause "thou canst not see," refusing to take it as a mere circumstantial addition and holding the line open between an affirmative and an interrogative sense. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the images into a picture of bewilderment: the guilty man is brought to his wits' end, amazed and lost, unable to see wherefore God contends with him, set as in a mist in the midst of dark waters; and Henry draws the sober rule that those who have shown no mercy may justly be denied the comfortable hope of finding mercy. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Eliphaz has described, with unconscious accuracy, the very darkness Job was in, while wholly mistaking its cause — reading as the just blinding of a hidden sinner what was in truth the tried darkness of a faithful man.
12:
"Is not God in the height of heaven? and behold the height of the stars, how high they are!" — Eliphaz lifts his eyes to the sky, and the witnesses watch him bend a true confession toward a false charge. The reformed John Gill dwells first on the plain glory of the words. Heaven takes its very name from its height; God dwells there as in the habitation of his holiness, his throne set in the heaven of heavens where he manifests his glory and the angels behold his face; and because this is the chief seat of his majesty, "heaven" comes to stand as one of his names. The clause may even be rendered, Gill notes, "is not God the height of the heavens?" or, with the Vulgate, "higher than the heavens" — above them all as their Creator.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the doctrine at face value: yes, God is in the height of heaven; no heaven is so high but he is there; and from this very truth Eliphaz rightly proves that a man cannot be profitable to God, ought not to contend with him, and should approach him with reverence. But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees where Eliphaz is really heading. He is attributing to Job an infidel inference from God's exaltation — as though Job held that God is so far above the heavens and stars, with so much dense ether and thick cloud between his throne and the earth, that he can neither see it nor its inhabitants. These were sentiments Job never held nor uttered, Clarke protests; "but if a man be dressed in a bear's skin, he may be hunted and worried by his own dogs."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the specific unbelief Eliphaz imputes — the practical atheism so often rebuked in the Psalms, which denies to the God of heaven a knowledge of earthly things, as Epicurus denied it to his blessed and unconcerned gods (Ps. 73:11; Ps. 94:7). John Wesley reads the height rather as the ground of God's oversight, from that high tower looking down to behold and govern and recompense all men's actions, and himself far higher than the stars from which he can easily see all. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Eliphaz begins from an orthodox truth — the transcendence of God — only to build upon it a slander, dressing Job in the skin of the very unbeliever whom the height of heaven ought to abash.
13:
The imagined creed is now put into Job's mouth as a word of defiance: "and thou sayest, How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud?" The reformed John Gill is careful to say what Job did and did not do. Job never said this with his lips; Eliphaz only supposed it to be the reasoning of his heart, an invidious consequence drawn from Job's remarks on the afflictions of the godly and the prosperity of the wicked. Because Job had questioned the neat distribution of reward and punishment, Eliphaz concluded that he must secretly deny providence altogether — must think that God, dwelling beyond the stars, cannot see what is done on earth, so that men may sin with impunity and never be called to account.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the supposed speech sharply — "So then thou thinkest: What doth God know? Can he judge through the thick cloud?" — and set it in its context as the charge that Job has joined the scoffers who fence off the heavens from the earth. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, whose comment reaches across these verses, protests the whole method. Eliphaz is attributing to Job blasphemous sentiments he never held, and then dilating upon them and drawing inferences injurious to his character; "Job's friends attribute falsities to him, and then draw inferences from them," a trick, Clarke observes tartly, that polemic writers in theology and politics have always been fond of.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the sin Eliphaz is describing and, in describing, half commits. To reason as Eliphaz supposes Job to reason is to hold the truth in unrighteousness, fighting against religion with its own weapons and turning God's own artillery upon itself; for bad men expel the fear of God from their hearts by first banishing the eye of God from the world, saying in effect that the Lord seeth not (Ezek. 8:12). The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the atheism here painted is real and dreadful, but that it is Eliphaz's invention and not Job's confession — a creed manufactured for the accused out of the raw material of his honest perplexity, that he might be condemned for denying the very providence whose strange dealings he was only struggling to understand. Gill is careful to add that the whole is Eliphaz's inference and not Job's word, drawn out of what Job had said of the afflictions of the godly and the prosperity of the wicked; and so the very perplexity that had driven Job toward God is turned, in his friend's hands, into evidence that he had thrust God away.
14:
The counterfeit creed is completed with a picture of a God shut in behind the sky: "thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven." The reformed John Gill exposes the false logic Eliphaz fathers on Job. It is the reasoning of atheistical men who make God altogether such a one as themselves: because thick clouds hide the sun and moon and stars from human sight, they fancy the clouds must hide men and their doings from the sight of God — whereas nothing whatever can come between God and man, and his eyes are upon all the ways of the sons of men.

The wesleyan-arminian voices give the imagined blasphemy its two forms. Adam Clarke reads the clause as the confining of God to his exalted regions — "he cares nothing for the inhabitants of the earth." John Wesley makes it the old error of the philosophers: God's delight is in heaven, which is worthy of his care, but he will not burden himself with the care of earth — the opinion, Wesley notes, of many heathen thinkers, which they falsely imagined to be Job's as well.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two suppositions side by side and answers both. Either Eliphaz supposes Job to think it impossible for God to see through the dark cloud that comes between — an absurdity, since distance of place is no difficulty to him who fills immensity; or to think it below God, a diminution of his glory, to take cognizance of this lower world, as though the government of it were a burden to the supreme governor. If the sun, a mere creature, can reach every corner of the earth with its light from that great height and through many a thick cloud, Henry argues, shall we question it of the Creator (Ps. 19:6)? The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the last clause vividly — "and in the vault of heaven he walketh at his pleasure" — the very image of a God who strolls the ramparts of the sky with no thought for the earth below. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Eliphaz has drawn a portrait of unbelief and hung Job's name beneath it, ascribing to a man who longed for God's presence the creed of men who wished God away. And here, they note, the argument doubles back on itself: the God whom Eliphaz pictures as too high and too cloud-wrapped to see is the very God whose all-seeing eye, rightly confessed, would abash the false accuser rather than the innocent accused.
15:
Leaving the invented creed, Eliphaz appeals to the warning of history: "hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden?" The reformed John Gill hears in "the old way" the whole ancient course of sin — the way of Cain and his descendants, of the old world whose every imagination was evil continually, whom Peter calls the world of the ungodly; men of wickedness who trod the paths of sin until they made them a beaten road, walking in them obstinately and proceeding from evil to evil. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the appeal its rhetorical force. Eliphaz would frighten Job into repentance by comparing his case with the sinners of the old world: "thy condition is bad now, but, unless thou repent, it will be worse, as theirs was" — theirs whom a flood swept away, and theirs, the men of Sodom, whom fire consumed, the two standing instances of God's wrath so often set together for warning (Luke 17:26; 2 Pet. 2:5-6). There is an old way, Henry grants, that wicked men have trodden — a broad, tracked, well-worn way — and it is good to mark it, but only that we may not dare to walk in it; Eliphaz's aim, however, is that Job may see his own face in that glass.

Here a shade of difference divides the witnesses. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott read the question not as a mild "consider their end" but as a fresh accusation. Clarke takes it as charging that Job walks the same way the wicked of old walked in; Ellicott renders it, "dost thou keep the old way which the wicked men trod? dost thou hold their tenets?" — so that the verse asks not whether Job has studied that road but whether he is on it. John Wesley keeps closer to Henry, glossing the phrase as "the way of antiquity, of men living in ancient times," and their end or success.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the substance, for whether Eliphaz bids Job mark the doom of the old world or charges him with sharing their path, the intent is one: to press upon him the terror of the flood and the fire, and to number him, by insinuation, among those whom such judgments swept away. And the reader knows what Eliphaz does not — that the man he is herding toward the company of the drowned and the burned is the one man of his age whom God had singled out as blameless.
16:
Eliphaz fixes on the fate of that ancient race: "which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overflown with a flood." The reformed John Gill lingers over "out of time." The men of the old world were sent into eternity before the common term of life, cut off in the midst of days when, by the long reckoning of those ages, many might have lived centuries more, which made their untimely extirpation the more dreadful; and the phrase may also mean "without time," suddenly and at unawares, cut down like trees by the axe or grass by the scythe. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads their "foundation" as the earth on which they built themselves and all their hopes, overflown by the flood brought in upon the world of the ungodly; those who build upon such sand, he warns, choose a foundation sure to be swept away when the rains descend and the floods come (Matt. 7:27).

The wesleyan-arminian voices tie the verse firmly to Noah's flood. Adam Clarke identifies these as the unrighteous of Noah's day, who said in effect to God, "Depart from us," and rejected the preacher's warning; John Wesley reads them as destroyed together with their foundation — the earth and all their supports in it — by the general deluge. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet, "who were withered up before their time, their foundation was poured out as a stream," keeping the picture of a life dried up and a ground washed away.

Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, agrees that the allusion is to the Flood — an allusion he thinks important for the great age of the book, since Job can hardly fail to be very old — but he offers a second, figurative sense of the last clause that the others do not. "Whose foundation became as a flowing stream" may mean that the principles of the wicked are infectious and bear all before them, like a river in flood. So a mild debate opens: whether the overflown foundation is simply the literal earth swept off by the deluge, as Gill, Henry, Clarke, and Wesley take it, or an image of corrupting principles that sweep a generation away, as Ellicott suggests. The witnesses do not divide over the warning itself; they agree that Eliphaz means the ruin of the antediluvians for a mirror of Job's own supposed end, and that the mirror is held up to the wrong man.
17:
The sin that drew down the flood is named as a word of contempt: "which said unto God, Depart from us: and what can the Almighty do for them?" The reformed John Gill reads the first clause as the language of men who would not be admonished, exhorted, instructed, or governed — who bade God be gone that they might live as they pleased. And he catches the irony that Job had used these very words of prosperous sinners, whereas Eliphaz turns them upon men who were cut off for their wickedness. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes that reversal explicit: Eliphaz repeats Job's words from the previous chapter "but to a contrary purpose," for Job had alleged them to show that such men prospered notwithstanding their impiety, and Eliphaz produces them to prove they were destroyed for it (ch. 21:14-15).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the harder second clause three ways. "What can the Almighty do for them?" may mark the justice of their punishment — men who bid God depart leave him nothing to do but cut them off; or it may voice the injustice of their sin, as if they asked what the Almighty had ever done against them, or wherein he had wearied them (Mic. 6:3; Jer. 2:5); or it may give the reason of their sin, a sneering doubt whether God can do them any good or harm at all, like those who say the Lord will not do good, neither will he do evil (Zeph. 1:12). The absurdity of it, Henry says, is exposed by the one word "Almighty": for if he be that, what can he not do?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the scene in Noah's day, when the men who had all things rejected the preacher with "What can the Almighty do for us? Let him do his worst"; and he notes that the Septuagint reads "to us" for "to them," quoting their own defiance directly. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that here again Eliphaz fathers upon Job the very thoughts Job had ascribed to the wicked, while Keil and Delitzsch render the taunt plainly, "Depart from us! and what can the Almighty do to them?" The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Eliphaz has taken Job's own honest description of the prosperous ungodly and flung it back as though it were Job's confession of fellowship with them.
18:
"Yet he filled their houses with good things: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me" — the verse joins an aggravation of the sin to a sudden protest of the speaker's own innocence, and the witnesses take up both. The reformed John Gill reads the first half as the measure of the ungodly's ingratitude: God had filled their houses with temporal good, with the plenty of his providence, for earthly enjoyments are good things in themselves when rightly used; and that he should so load with benefits the very men who said "what can the Almighty do for us?" is the deep aggravation of their contempt.

On the second half the witnesses hear a barb. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke shows Eliphaz sarcastically quoting Job's own words back at him — "but the counsel of the wicked is far from me" — the very phrase Job had used, now turned so that Eliphaz, having ranked Job among the impious he has been describing, may say in effect, "Thank God I have no part with you nor your creed" (ch. 21:16). The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that the bitterness of the irony here reaches its climax, in that Eliphaz adopts the very formula of repudiation Job had himself used. John Wesley hears the same reflection: Eliphaz repeats Job's words "not without reflection — thou didst say so, but against thy own principle," and adds that he who had observed God's terrible judgments on the wicked has far more reason to abhor their counsels than Job had.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the protest more kindly, as a sincere disowning of atheism in which even quarrelling friends may unite. Job had said the counsel of the wicked was far from him, and Eliphaz will not be behind him; for those who differ in some matters of religion ought still to stand together against irreligion, and not let their disputes cool their zeal in that common cause. And Henry draws the warning from the aggravation: many have their houses full of good things but their hearts empty of grace, and are thereby marked for ruin. The witnesses do not divide over the meaning; most hear Eliphaz's closing phrase as a taunt that throws Job's language in his teeth, while Henry hears in it a truer note — a shared abhorrence of the ungodliness both men, for all their strife, sincerely renounce.
19:
The destruction of the wicked becomes, in this verse, the joy of the godly: "the righteous see it, and are glad: and the innocent laugh them to scorn." The reformed John Gill is quick to guard the gladness from cruelty. What the righteous rejoice in is not the counsel or the prosperity of the wicked but their ruin — and even that not as the mere misery of fellow-creatures, which it would be brutish and inhuman to relish, but because they themselves have been kept from such sins and delivered from such oppressors, and chiefly because of the glory of the divine perfections, the holiness and justice of God made manifest.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse beside the close of many a psalm, where the long-delayed triumph of God's retributive justice at last breaks out to the joy of those who had suffered innocently; the thing the righteous "see," they explain, is that very manifestation, and the scorn falls on the ungodly whose mocking pride comes to an ignominious end (Ps. 58:11). The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it simply: the righteous see God's judgments on the incorrigibly wicked and know that the Judge of all the earth does right, and so they rejoice in all the dispensations of his providence. The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, refers the sight, like the flood and the fire before it, to the destruction of the wicked as in the days of Noah.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same thought and gives the laughter its holy warrant. The righteous shall observe the ruin of the wicked and be glad — not to see their fellows miserable, nor for any private turn served, but to see God glorified, his word fulfilled, the power of oppressors broken, and fair warning given to all others; and they may laugh them to scorn as God himself does, in a holy manner, exposing the folly of those who made not God their strength (Ps. 2:4; Prov. 1:26). Some, Henry adds, would read it of righteous Noah rejoicing over the drowned world, and of Lot over Sodom. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the joy is real and pure, a delight in justice and not in suffering — even as they know that Eliphaz means it, cruelly, to make Job feel himself the object of that scorn rather than a sharer in that gladness.
20:
The triumph-song of the righteous is quoted, and its wording sets the witnesses debating who speaks it: "whereas our substance is not cut down, but the remnant of them the fire consumeth." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the line as the very shout of the innocent over the fallen — "verily our opponent is destroyed, and the fire hath devoured their abundance" — the fire being that which fell on Sodom. Charles Ellicott takes it likewise as the words of the righteous and innocent of the previous verse, rendering it, "surely they that did rise up against us are cut off, and the remnant of them the fire hath consumed," and judging the Authorized Version's turn less correct.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the two great judgments in view. Adam Clarke paraphrases, "we who fear the Lord still continue in health and peace, whereas they who departed from him are destroyed even to their remnant," and notes Mr. Good's reading of "our tribe" for "our substance"; the flood took the ungodly in Noah's day, and their remnant the fire in Lot's. John Wesley marks how Eliphaz changes the person to "our," ranking himself among the righteous, and reads the "remnant" as all that the general calamity left undestroyed, the "fire" as Sodom and Gomorrah: a man may find here and there an instance of a wicked man dying in peace, but what is that against the drowning of a whole world and the burning of the cities of the plain?

Yet another reading turns the verse from a hymn of the innocent into a self-congratulation of the friends. The reformed John Gill allows that "our substance is not cut down" may be Eliphaz and his companions contrasting their own unbroken estate with Job's, the difference being that they were righteous and he wicked; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes it just so, hearing the friends say, "our substance is not cut down as thine is; we prosper, a sign we are the favourites of Heaven." The very rule by which Eliphaz condemns Job, Henry notes, serves him to magnify himself — a deceitful rule, for none knows love or hatred by all that is before him; when others are consumed and we are not, we ought rather to be thankful and take warning than to censure them and exalt ourselves. So the debate stands over the speaker: whether the verse is the pure triumph-song of the innocent over the wicked, or Eliphaz's smug comparison of his own prosperity with Job's ruin; and spoken by Eliphaz, the witnesses agree, it is a boast built on a false measure.
21:
"Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace: thereby good shall come unto thee" — with these words the storm of accusation gives way to counsel, and the witnesses breathe more freely. The reformed John Gill notes the change of temper: from severe charges Eliphaz turns to advice and exhortation, and speaks now in a kinder strain, though still on the false supposition that Job is a bad man estranged from God. The word supposes an unacquaintance with God — the natural state of every man from the womb — and acquaintance with him, Gill says, begins at conversion and is carried on by prayer and by attendance on his worship and ordinances.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry can "almost forgive Eliphaz his hard censures" for the sake of this good counsel, than which nothing could be better said. Out of the same mouth, he marvels, both sweet and bitter proceed; and he takes the occasion to teach that ministers must deal both ways with men — speaking from Mount Sinai by the terrors of the law and from Mount Sion by the comforts of the gospel. "Acquaint now thyself with God," he urges: acquiesce in his providence, join thyself to his interest, and be no longer a stranger to him; "be at peace" — at peace with thyself, not fretful and uneasy, and at peace with God, reconciled and no longer carrying on this unholy war, for how can two walk together except they be agreed (Amos 3:3)?

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the verb, which is the same sakan whose sense they had traced at v.2: in its causative form it means to be on friendly terms with one, to grow accustomed to him, and so they render, "make friends now with him, so hast thou peace." The wesleyan-arminian voices add their own colour. Adam Clarke suggests the verb may rather mean "treasure up, lay up" — lay up now an interest with God and be at peace, get the divine favour, and "thereby," in these two things, good shall come to thee. John Wesley expands the summons into a whole return: renew thy acquaintance with God by prayer, repentance, humiliation, and hearty compliance with his commands, for it is our honour that we are made capable of this acquaintance, our misery that by sin we lost it, and our privilege that through Christ we may return to it. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, notes that Eliphaz here does only what he had done in chapter 5 and Zophar in chapter 11 — turns from threatening to advice — and reads the promise as "thereby shall thine increase be good." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the counsel is excellent in itself and only marred by its address, offered as a cure for an estrangement that, in Job's case, did not exist.
22:
The counsel continues with a call to submission: "receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in thine heart." The reformed John Gill doubts that the law of Moses can be meant, since it is a question whether that law yet was, or could have reached Job; he takes "the law" rather as any doctrine, any revelation of God's mind made to the patriarchs and handed down, to be received as the word of God with meekness and reverence, and not only heard but obeyed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as the heart of a sinner's conversion — to receive the law from God's mouth and no longer from the world and the flesh; we receive our being, our maintenance, and our hope from God, and from him too we must receive law, saying, "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" (Acts 9:6); and it is not enough to receive the word, we must retain it, laying it up in the heart as a thing of great price.

Here the witnesses divide over that word "law," the Hebrew torah. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will have nothing of the notion that only the Noahic precepts or the law of nature are meant — "stuff and vanity!" — insisting that the allusion is plainly to the law afterward given by Moses, called emphatically the Law, containing his very words. Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott inclines the other way. It would be deeply interesting, he says, to know whether the Torah is here alluded to; but since Job seems the one Gentile book of the Old Testament, touching the world at large, it is likelier prior to the Law, or written in independence of it, the life it depicts being that of patriarchal times — though he owns the difficulty of knowing what "his words" could mean before the Mosaic revelation, unless as a witness to that inner voice of God in the conscience which the holy in every age have known.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, renders the couplet, "receive now teaching from his mouth, and place his utterances in thy heart," and John Wesley reads it to the same effect: take the rule of thy whole life not from thy own imaginations but from God, from his law written in the mind and the instruction of holy men, and let it sink from the ear into the heart. So the debate is genuine — whether the "law" Eliphaz names is the Mosaic Torah, with Clarke, or an older patriarchal revelation, with Gill and Ellicott, a question bound up with the great age of the book. The witnesses do not divide over the exhortation itself, which all own to be good: that a man make God's word the rule of his heart.
23:
The promise now hangs on a plain condition: "if thou return to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up, thou shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacles." The reformed John Gill hears in "return" the confession of a prior departure, a backsliding to be repented of; and he finds encouragement in the very name Eliphaz uses, Shaddai, the Almighty, which signifies the all-sufficient One, whose grace is sufficient to receive returning sinners, pardon their sins, supply their wants, and preserve them to the end. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar of conversion: the phrase is "return unto" the Almighty, the construction used of a thorough and complete turning, and the verb "be built up" is used here of prosperity raised again from its ruins, as a fallen house is rebuilt (Jer. 24:6).

The wesleyan-arminian voices spell out what the building means. Adam Clarke: God will restore Job to his former prosperity, and he shall again have a household — not of servants only but of children. John Wesley marks the emphatic Hebrew, which implies a thorough turning from sin to God, so as to love him and cleave to him; and he weighs the last clause two ways, either as a spiritual promise, that God will give grace to reform, or as a temporal one, that Job shall put away the very punishment of his sins far from all his dwellings.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lets the clause betray the assumption beneath the kindness: "thou shalt put away iniquity" implies all along the imputation of apostasy and iniquity to Job. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole as sound counsel, urging Job not only to turn from sin but to turn home to God by a universal reformation, and to put away iniquity far from his tabernacle — the very advice Zophar had given (ch. 11:14) — for family reformation is a needful reformation, and we and our house must serve the Lord. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the promise of restoration on repentance is true and gracious in the abstract, and cruelly misapplied in the particular, since it silently presumes the very guilt in Job that the whole book denies. Gill draws comfort even from the misdirected word, that the name Almighty holds out to any real backslider a grace sufficient to receive and restore him; and Wesley adds that the turning here required is no half-motion but a hearty devoting of the whole self to God's fear and service, the return of a man who means to cleave to him and not merely to edge toward him.
24:
"Then shalt thou lay up gold as dust, and the gold of Ophir as the stones of the brooks" — the promise turns to riches, and the witnesses divide over whether it offers gold or bids Job despise it. On the first reading the words foretell an overflowing wealth. The reformed John Gill takes them so — Job shall have such plenty of gold as not to be counted — and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, though he shows how widely the versions differ (Montanus, the Vulgate's "flint for earth and torrents of gold for flint," Calmet, Good, and Coverdale all rendering it another way), leaves the plain drift as an increase of treasure.

On the second reading the verse is not a promise of gold but a command to reckon it worthless. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses this sense: "put thy treasure on a level with the dust, and the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks" — that is, count it of no more value than such stones, and do not set thy heart upon it; and he hears beneath it the insinuation that the wealth for which Job was famous had been the accumulation of wrong-doing. The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, renders the couplet the same way — "lay by in the dust the gold ore, and under the pebbles of the brooks the gold of Ophir" — so that Job is bidden to resign his earthly treasure before the true recompense of the next verse. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both senses together: Job shall lay up gold, and yet "not as his treasure and portion, but as dust," valuing it so little that he lays it at his feet rather than in his bosom, for wealth is a blessing indeed only when we are not ensnared with the love of it.

So the debate runs between abundance and contempt — is Job promised heaps of gold, or told to hold gold as dust? — and the witnesses do not wholly resolve it, though the weight of the grammatical-historical reading, and Henry's reconciling turn, lean toward the nobler sense: that the reward of return is not more gold but a heart set free from it. Ellicott adds that the very site of Ophir, whose gold was proverbial, has always been disputed, some placing it in India, some in southern Arabia, some on the coast of Africa; but the point the witnesses seize is not the geography of the gold, but the low place a returning man is to give it.
25:
The reward rises from the gold to the Giver of gold: "yea, the Almighty shall be thy defence, and thou shalt have plenty of silver." The witnesses divide over the first clause, for the Hebrew word may be read either "defence" or "gold." The reformed John Gill gives both: God shall be Job's defence, securing his wealth by his providence and preserving his soul from every enemy, a wall of fire about him; or, as others render it, "the Almighty shall be thy gold," bidding Job treat earthly riches with contempt and reckon God himself his truest treasure, whose grace is better than gold that perishes (1 Pet. 1:7). The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the second reading for one of his finest strokes: the same word rendered "gold" in the previous verse stands here, so that "worldlings make gold their god, and saints make God their gold"; those enriched with his favour and grace have abundance of the best gold, and best laid up, and a defence against all the Sabeans and Chaldeans that ever spoiled a man.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott comes down for the richer rendering: rather than "thy defence," read "the Almighty shall be thy treasure, and precious silver unto thee"; the rare word qualifying silver, he notes, occurs only three other times in Scripture — of "the strength of the hills" and "the strength of a unicorn" — its root idea being brightness or splendour. The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, renders to the same effect, "so shall the Almighty be to thee gold ore in abundance, and silver to thee of the brightest lustre."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the promise of silver plain, but he will not let Eliphaz's underlying doctrine pass unchallenged: for beneath the fine words lies the belief that "to those whom God loves best he gives the most earthly good — the rich and the great are his high favourites, the poor and distressed he holds for his enemies." That, Clarke sees, is the false theology of the whole speech. So the witnesses divide over the word — defence or treasure — but converge on the sweeter sense that God himself is the reward, even while Clarke marks how Eliphaz cheapens it by binding God's favour so tightly to gold and silver. The best gold, they agree, is the Almighty; the error is to measure his love by the meaner kind.
26:
From wealth the promise climbs to a higher blessing: "for then shalt thou have thy delight in the Almighty, and shalt lift up thy face unto God." The reformed John Gill makes the delight the fruit of a whole reordering of the heart — a delight in the perfections of God's nature, his works, his word and worship, and in communion with him — which can only come when Job is better acquainted with God and his affections are taken off earthly riches, when he has learned to look on gold as dust and to make God his gold; then, and not till then, could he have true complacency in the Almighty. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry ties the verse back to the last: thus the Almighty comes to be Job's gold, by his delighting in him as worldly men delight in their money; for the way to have our heart's desire is to make God our heart's delight (Ps. 37:4), and then a man may lift up his face to God with boldness, as those do whose hearts condemn them not (1 John 3:21).

The grammatical-historical voices keep the wording. Charles Ellicott notes that Zophar had already promised Job the same thing, that he should lift up his face without spot (ch. 11:15); Keil and Delitzsch render, "for then thou shalt delight thyself in the Almighty, and lift up thy countenance to Eloah." John Wesley glosses the last clause briefly — "look up to him with cheerfulness and confidence."

But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke halts at the doctrine Eliphaz has folded into the promise. To make Job's delight in God turn on his restored prosperity — "thou shalt know from thy temporal prosperity that God favours thee" — is, Clarke protests, a gospel very unlike that of Paul and John, who taught that the justified have peace with God, that the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are his children, and that we may even glory in tribulation, which itself is often a mark of God's favour rather than its withdrawal. Here the witnesses do part company: most expound the delight and the lifted face as the true joy of a soul reconciled, while Clarke stands apart to warn that Eliphaz has bound that joy to the wrong evidence, measuring the smile of God by the return of goods rather than by the peace of a pardoned conscience.
27:
The restored fellowship shows itself in answered prayer: "thou shalt make thy prayer unto him, and he shall hear thee, and thou shalt pay thy vows." The reformed John Gill hears in the word a supplication that pleads not merit but mercy, offered for the Lord's mercy's sake and for the sake of Christ's righteousness, and offered often, for the term implies a multiplying of prayer; and this, he adds, is set down not as a bare duty but as a privilege and a benefit, the very access of a child to a Father through the Mediator. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the Hebrew, "thou shalt open," or unbosom, thyself: when the heart prays, God hears; and the man, being blessed, vows fidelity, prays on, and is enabled to pay what he vowed.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the promise, "if thou prayest to him, he will hear thee, and thou shalt pay thy vows," reading it as the first of a chain of blessings that runs on through the devising of plans and the lifting up of the fallen in the verses to come. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, marks the same multiplying of prayer — "under all thy burdens, in all thy wants, cares, and fears, thou shalt send to heaven for wisdom, strength, and comfort" — and reads the paying of vows as the obtaining of the very blessings for which the vows were made.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into a picture of steady correspondence with heaven, letters going up and answers coming down. By prayer, he says, Job shall send his petitions to God, who will never think them troublesome though many and long, for the oftener we come to the throne of grace the more welcome; God will answer by his providence and grace, giving what is asked in kind or in kindness; and then, by his praises, Job shall reply to the mercies received and pay his vows, for when God performs what in distress we prayed for, we must make conscience of performing what we then promised (Ps. 116:14). The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the mark of the reconciled man is this free traffic of prayer and answer, and that Eliphaz, for all the falseness of his premise, here describes a real and blessed thing — the confidence of a heart that may ask and be heard.
28:
The blessing spreads from prayer to purpose: "thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee: and the light shall shine upon thy ways." The reformed John Gill first guards the words from overstatement, for strictly this belongs only to God, whose decrees are unfrustrable, while man appoints and God disappoints; but he allows the promise to Job in a threefold sense — as a magistrate, whose righteous sentences shall stand; as a private man, prospered in his designs; or, best, as a praying man, whose purposes, committed to God, are brought to pass. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps it short and dependent: "whatsoever thou purposest in his strength, thou shalt be enabled to accomplish."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears an echo of a great instance behind the promise — the memorable case of Abraham's intercession for Sodom, to which, he thinks, there is not improbably an allusion here, so that the decreeing of a thing shades into the prevailing prayer of a righteous man for others. The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, renders the couplet, "and thou devisest a plan, and it shall be established to thee, and light shineth upon thy ways," reading it as the settled success of a man at peace with God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the inward calm of it. Job shall frame all his projects with such wisdom and resignation to God's will that the issue shall be to his heart's content; let him commit his works to the Lord, and his thoughts shall be established (Prov. 16:3); and where he now complains of darkness round about him, the light shall then shine on his ways, God's wisdom his guide and his favour his comfort. John Wesley reads the two clauses together — the purposes not disappointed but ratified by God, and in all his counsels and actions the light of divine direction, comfort, and success. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse promises the deep repose of a life brought into accord with God's will, so that a man's plans prosper and his path is lit — a repose real and desirable in itself, though offered to Job as if his present darkness were the fruit of a sin he had not committed. And Ellicott's glance at Abraham lends the promise a further reach, for the man reconciled to God decrees not for himself alone but, like the friend of God pleading over Sodom, may prevail in prayer for others — a hint, the reader sees, of the very office Job himself will fill when the book is done.
29:
Even a time of general calamity is turned to hope: "when men are cast down, then thou shalt say, There is lifting up; and he shall save the humble person." The reformed John Gill takes the cast-down as the wicked brought low from prosperity into straits and difficulties, against whose fall the returning Job shall stand secure. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it more inwardly and more sweetly: when men round about are cast down in their affairs and in their spirits, sinking toward despair, Job shall find in himself that which not only bears him up under his troubles but lifts him above them; for when men's hearts fail them for fear, the disciples of God may lift up their heads for joy (Luke 21:26-28), since God will save the humble, and those that humble themselves shall be exalted.

Over the exact turn of the words, however, the witnesses divide. Most read Job's word as a cheerful assurance — "there is lifting up." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders it almost as a command of faith, "when they shall humble themselves, thou shalt say, Be exalted; for the downcast of eye he will save," hearing the very sentiment of the gospel, that he who humbles himself shall be exalted; and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch likewise take the cry as an imperative, "if they are cast down, thou sayest, Arise! and him that hath low eyes he saveth." But the other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, records a harsher possibility: some understand the clause in a bad sense, so that when men are cast down Job shall say, "It was pride that caused their fall" — a verdict on the proud rather than a lifting of the low.

John Wesley keeps to the kindlier reading — in a time of general calamity, when all around are cast down, God will deliver Job. So the debate is over the temper of the words: whether Job's saying is a promise of exaltation to the humble, a summons to the fallen to rise, or a judgment pronounced on the pride that cast them down. The witnesses do not finally resolve it, but the weight of them falls on grace — that the God who saves the man of lowly eyes will lift up his servant even when the world is sinking — and they leave the reader to feel the pathos that this radiant promise is spoken to a man already humbled to the dust, whom Eliphaz still supposes to need humbling.
30:
The speech ends on a note that, unknown to the speaker, prophesies its own undoing: "he shall deliver the island of the innocent: and it is delivered by the pureness of thine hands." The words are famously obscure, and the witnesses labour over them. The reformed John Gill asks bluntly where such an "island of innocent persons" is to be found, and offers a better sense — "the innocent shall deliver the island," good men saving a whole country by their counsel and their prayers; but he notes that the little word rendered "island" is really a negative particle meaning "not," so that the phrase may point to "him that is not innocent."

That grammatical thread the grammatical-historical voices take up in earnest. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the reading "the not-guiltless," which at first seems to mean Job himself in his present condition, a mild periphrasis for the guilty man who has merited his suffering; they set the whole verse at the head of the third course of the controversy, in which the friends, having withdrawn their earlier promises, now hold out deliverance only on the terms of repentance. Charles Ellicott declares "the island of the innocent" undoubtedly an error for "he shall deliver him that is not innocent": even the guilty shall be delivered by the cleanness of Job's hands, as the ten righteous would have saved Sodom. And here Ellicott hears the deep irony of the ending, for this last word of Eliphaz has the force of a prophecy — it is exactly thus that the history of Job closes, when Eliphaz himself, no longer innocent, is pardoned through Job's intercession (ch. 42:8-9).

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the same drift. Adam Clarke takes "island" for an Arabic particle meaning "any," and renders, "he shall deliver every innocent person; the innocent shall be delivered by the pureness of thy hands" — the word "island," he insists, must be given up as making no sense; and he closes his account of Eliphaz with a stern verdict, that a man who began with the bitterest charges and ended with commonplace exhortations has left us scarcely one new maxim, so that we may bless God for Moses and the prophets. John Wesley reads the promise as fulfilled to the letter: God will have such respect to Job's innocency that for his sake he will deliver others, even those ripe for destruction, by his prayers from a pure heart — as indeed Eliphaz and his friends, themselves not innocent, were at the last delivered by the pureness of Job's hands (ch. 42:8). The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, inclining to "the innocent shall deliver the island," makes the lesson plain — a good man is a public good, and sinners fare the better for the saints among them. So the witnesses divide over the wording — whether it be the innocent delivering a land, or the guilty delivered for a righteous man's sake, or every innocent one saved — but they gather, at the speech's close, on a truth Eliphaz spoke better than he knew: that the pure hands he doubted would prove, in the end, the very hands that saved him.
